Newborn Russian desman pups are remarkably altricial, with a recorded wet weight at birth of only 3.3 grams [Wwb = 3.3 grams]. This modest neonatal mass places them among the smaller offspring relative to adult size within the family Talpidae, a pattern that reflects the species' energetically costly semi-aquatic lifestyle. Following a gestation period that typically spans approximately 47.5 days [tg = approximately 47.5 days] at the species' normal body temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C], females give birth to a litter ranging from one to five pups [N_R_i = a litter ranging from one to five pups]. The short gestation, relative to other small mammals of comparable adult mass, suggests a trade-off favoring rapid embryonic development to maximize the number of litters produced within a single active season. Indeed, females are capable of raising two litters per year [F_R_i = two litters per year], a reproductive frequency that, when combined with the observed litter size, yields a substantial annual reproductive output for an insectivore of this size. This strategy is likely an adaptation to high juvenile mortality rates in the dynamic floodplain ecosystems the desman inhabits.

The period of lactation and maternal care is relatively extended for a mammal of this size, with weaning occurring at 30 days after birth [tx = 30 days after birth] when measured at the standard thermoneutral body temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C] for this species. At the point of nutritional independence, the young desman attains a wet weight at weaning of approximately 265 grams [Wwx = approximately 265 grams], representing a substantial increase from the neonatal mass. This nearly eighty-fold increase in body mass over a single month underscores the intense parental investment required to bring offspring to a size where they can begin to forage independently. The weaning weight is a critical life-history threshold, as it must be sufficient to support the juvenile through the challenging transition to solid food and, ultimately, to a semi-aquatic existence. During this suckling juvenile stage, the pups remain entirely dependent on the mother's milk, and their growth trajectory closely tracks the availability of aquatic invertebrates that sustain the lactating female.

Sexual maturity in the Russian desman is not achieved quickly; the time since birth at puberty is estimated at approximately 320 days after birth [tp = approximately 320 days after birth] at a body temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C], a value derived from comparative scaling relationships with other talpid species. This prolonged period of juvenile development is unusual for an insectivore of its body size and likely reflects the complex ecological and physiological demands of mastering a semi-aquatic foraging niche. Before reaching reproductive maturity, young individuals must attain a sufficient body mass and develop the specialized sensory and locomotor skills necessary for efficient underwater prey capture. Consequently, the juvenile phase is marked by a continued accumulation of body reserves, bringing the individual close to the ultimate adult body mass. This extended maturation period acts as a demographic bottleneck, filtering out individuals unable to navigate the seasonal challenges of flooding, ice cover, and prey availability that characterize the desman's riparian habitat.

Adults of the Russian desman reach an ultimate wet weight of around 470 grams [Wwi = around 470 grams], although field studies report a typical range spanning from 380 to 520(380-520 grams [Wwi = 380-520 grams]) grams, with considerable variation linked to seasonal fat deposition and geographic locality. This impressive body size, making the desman the largest extant member of the family Talpidae in Eurasia, is a key adaptation for life in cold water, as a larger body volume confers a lower surface-area-to-volume ratio and thus reduces heat loss. The persistence of this metabolic strategy requires a high and consistent intake of prey, predominantly aquatic invertebrates such as amphipods and insect larvae. Even as a reproductively active adult, the species maintains an active thermoregulatory profile, with a core body temperature of 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C] being the physiological norm against which many of its life-history parameters are calibrated. This constant high body temperature is energetically expensive, necessitating efficient insulation in the form of dense, waterproof fur.

The natural lifespan of the Russian desman in its native environment is relatively short, with the maximum recorded longevity reaching approximately 1,825 days [am = approximately 1,825 days] at 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C], which corresponds to about five years. This lifespan is typical for a small- to medium-sized insectivorous mammal facing significant predation pressure from raptors, otters, and large piscivorous fish, as well as the inherent risks of unpredictable flood events along the Volga, Don, and Ural river basins. Captive records corroborate this figure, suggesting that physiological senescence begins to take effect beyond this age, even when individuals are protected from predation and resource limitation. Given the modest maximum reproductive rate implied by producing two litters per year with up to five pups each, the species relies on a relatively high annual fecundity to offset the high mortality rates experienced across all age classes. The life-history strategy of the Russian desman is thus a delicate balance between rapid, multi-litter reproduction and an extended, skill-intensive juvenile period, all sustained by the constant metabolic demand of its 38.3 °C [T = 38.3 °C] body temperature.
